title: Six Years On, Why Do Chinese Audiences Still Think Avatar Can't Be Topped?
excerpt: Chinese fans file Avatar under “once in a lifetime” releases, which has baffled a lot of overseas media. What secret about China's film market lies behind that?
body:
Chinese fans call *Avatar* a “will-I-live-to-see-it” franchise, which has baffled a lot of overseas media. What secret about China's film market lies behind that?

In mid-April, James Cameron announced he would make four more *Avatar* films, opening in the Christmas seasons of 2018, 2020, 2022 and 2023.

No leads have been cast, and the plot is still unclear. But a Weibo account called “Avatar 2” already shows 25.988 million views, and more than 200,000 people on Maoyan have marked the film “want to see” — about the same as *Warcraft*, which opens on June 8.

![A Weibo account for Avatar 2](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607031517357iDgpVG4Xt0KcfyS.jpg-w600)

![Maoyan “want to see” counts for Avatar 2](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703151736CbeyUIkY6NF0fBJo.jpg-w600)

![Maoyan “want to see” counts for Warcraft](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703151736kmRbv70zStyTOVLM.jpg-w600)

[*The Hollywood Reporter* was surprised by how enthusiastically Chinese moviegoers greeted the news of an *Avatar* sequel](http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/how-james-camerons-four-avatar-885479), and in fact it is still marveling at the box-office miracle *Avatar* pulled off when it opened in 2010. China's entire film market took in just 10.172 billion yuan that year, and *Avatar* alone accounted for 13.9% of it.

From there it ran a simple comparison: if *Avatar* could take the same share in 2016, it would earn $1.33 billion in China, while *Star Wars: The Force Awakens* (hereafter *Star Wars 7*) took only $936 million in North America.

*The Hollywood Reporter* used *Star Wars 7* for the comparison because the series is a national classic in the United States. What puzzled the magazine was why Chinese audiences don't love *Star Wars* yet treat *Avatar* as an extraordinary film.

“It's been seven years since *Avatar 1*, and I've been waiting for the sequel the whole time,” wrote the Weibo user @I Love My Lazy Little One. Under the same post, @John Knight replied: “I'll be 30 by 2023, and by then I'll bring my son or daughter along.” Plenty of people joked about the “will-I-live-to-see-it” franchise; others grumbled that “Cameron will probably miss the date.”

![Weibo comments about the Avatar sequels](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703151736rxCeV9lszfdnom60.jpg-w600)

![More Weibo comments about the Avatar sequels](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703151737Pvx0MBghQoWINU7R.jpg-w600)

But *Star Wars 7*, which Americans love, struggled to draw that kind of attention on Chinese social media, even though Disney did plenty of pre-release promotion, including hiring Lu Han as a spokesman. Data from the social-media analytics firm Lamplight shows that despite China's enormous online population, chatter about *Star Wars* there lags far behind Japan and South Korea, fellow Asian countries. And since *Star Wars 7* left theaters, it has become a rare sight on social media. *Rogue One: A Star Wars Story*, which opens in China in January 2017, has just over 20,000 “want to see” marks on Maoyan — *Avatar 2* has nearly ten times as many.

[QDaily has analyzed why *Star Wars* is not a good IP in China](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/16627.html): it missed the good years of China's film market, it lacks a mass base, and its fans' ages overlap poorly with the mainstream moviegoing crowd. Given all that, its failure there was inevitable.

That still doesn't answer the American puzzlement over why *Avatar* is held in such regard. And that isn't the only reason we're bringing *Avatar* up again. We also think it's worth asking why, after so long, it is still this popular, and what relationship a single film has with China's entire film market.

## Avatar Arrived Just as China's Film Market Was Taking Off

Pushed along by *Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon* and *Hero*, and above all by the market reforms that began in 2002 — when film distribution and exhibition left government control and went to the market — Chinese cinema entered its era of land grabs. Land grabs literally: before long the property developer Wanda joined in, and the screen count kept rising as commercial plazas went up.

In 2003 China had only 2,296 screens, and it was not until 2006 that the number barely passed 3,000. After that it shot past 4,000, and by 2009, the year before *Avatar* opened, it was approaching 5,000. That is why some people in the industry date the real boom in China's film market to 2009.

![A chart of China's growing screen count](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607031517383JYeOQKGnmgL7qBh.jpg-w600)

More screens meant more box office, and the annual record kept falling. *Titanic* held China's box-office record for 11 years, until 2009 — the year four films (*2012*, *Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen*, *The Founding of a Republic*) each took in more than 400 million yuan.

Then came *Avatar*'s 1.38 billion yuan. That year's runner-up, *Let the Bullets Fly*, took as much as 665 million yuan, and the annual total passed 10 billion yuan for the first time.

Cameron has a real bond with Chinese audiences. *Titanic* was how many people first learned the name James Cameron, and it arrived just as China was discovering that such a thing as the “blockbuster” existed, which is why its box-office peak stood unmatched for years. “My Heart Will Go On” and the shot of the two leads embracing at the bow both became a collective memory for a generation of moviegoers. When the *Titanic* 3D re-release reached China in 2012, it took more than 946 million yuan — more than twice its North American gross.

## Avatar Was Many People's First IMAX

Plenty of people still remember the scramble for tickets that *Avatar* set off — one film produced things that look, in hindsight, close to crazy.

Because a first time is always unforgettable.

“Now that's a blockbuster,” many viewers sighed. A blockbuster is really a spectacle: in the theater it has to make the audience scream and gasp, manufacture pleasure, and hand them two hours sealed off from reality.

In *Avatar*'s marketing, the core selling point was “3D plus IMAX delivers an experience no one has had before.”

IMAX, 3D, motion capture and the rest were industry jargon that audiences rarely cared about. Because of *Avatar*, those words turned into selling points.

![A crowd outside an IMAX screening of Avatar](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703151738NWk6EcUhqP3iHCGA.jpg-w600)

The images *Avatar* put on screen were beyond anything audiences had imagined. Being there, dreamlike, real and unreal — viewers reached for all kinds of words to describe it. And it was an experience available only in a theater: starting with *Avatar*, many people even settled into a habit of “3D and IMAX blockbusters at the cinema, ordinary movies at the computer.”

At the time both 3D and IMAX were scarce. Many cities had one or two theaters with 3D, and IMAX screens were rare nationwide. The China National Film Museum in Beijing had a 21-by-27-meter film IMAX screen, and it was the only place in northern China that could show the 70mm print of *Avatar*, so people queued in the cold wind first thing in the morning — the museum sits outside the Fifth Ring Road, which means a two-hour round trip by car, and that's without traffic.

Only five cinemas in the country could project the film IMAX version of *Avatar*. There were 22 IMAX screens in all, 11 of them commercial, roughly 0.2% of China's screens then.

Scarcity made it more desirable. A Nanning netizen calling himself “Clockwork Orange” flew to Dongguan just to catch the IMAX *Avatar*; on the night of February 14, Valentine's Day, Shanghai's Peace Cinema raised IMAX *Avatar* tickets to 288 yuan each and still sold 159 of them.

*Avatar* was where many people started watching IMAX, and it became a synonym for IMAX itself. It was also where IMAX's expansion in China started: by the end of 2015 mainland China had more than 290 IMAX theaters, and Greater China revenue reached $110.6 million.

But a first experience always leaves the deeper mark.

## Weibo's Fast Growth Helped Make the Memory Special

When *Avatar* opened, Jiang Defu of China Film Group's marketing and planning arm said the film “didn't do much marketing, at least not much more inside China.” “Build a dedicated official website, cook up gossip and scoops, hold media meet-and-greets, stage a global premiere” — that was the familiar playbook for film marketing then, and internet channels counted only as a supplement.

Even *Avatar*'s own publicists probably didn't grasp how its word of mouth was fermenting and erupting on social media. Part of why so many people hold a special memory of it is that it became a trending topic on Weibo. “Tickets are impossible to get,” “It's stunning,” “Only IMAX gives you the complete *Avatar*” — everyone was sharing how they felt on Weibo.

Sina Weibo, launched in 2009 and inspired by Facebook and Twitter, is seen as the start of Chinese social media. It grew fast from the beginning, and by 2010 its registered accounts had passed 100 million. Weibo was new to most people back then, and they were eager to use it to speak and to share everything in their lives.

*Avatar* happened to catch Weibo on the way up. It first brought in film people like Lu Chuan and Huang Jianxin, whose reviews then traveled widely online and in traditional media, forming the film's first word of mouth. Even habitual contrarians such as Li Chengpeng and Han Han praised its quality with one voice, and handed it talking points like “the most hardcore nail house ever.” Thanks to these big accounts, *Avatar*'s reputation spread quickly among the young people who make up the core of the audience.

Renren was still popular with students that year, and it contributed its share of reposts and comments too.

## In the End, Because That's When Today's Mainstream Moviegoers Started Going to the Movies

What do audiences like to watch?

Before answering that, answer this: who is watching movies?

In 2010, viewers aged 18 to 29 made up 64% of the audience, and those aged 30 to 45 made up 23%. A survey five years later showed the 18-to-29 share down to 45%, with the 30-to-45 group taking almost half.

That doesn't mean young viewers are disappearing. As time passed, the audience moved inevitably into the next age bracket, but the generational handover isn't finished, so the moviegoing habits formed back then haven't faded.

Seen that way, the people who were *Avatar* fans then are still the mainstream film audience now. That explains why, six years on, it is still this popular. A film's mainstream audience decides its taste and the direction it develops in.

Back to the question every studio strains to answer — what do audiences like to watch? — *Avatar*'s box office seems to make it easy: audiences like watching *Avatar*.

![A scene from Avatar](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703151739j7YE93rz4DNWKqcs.jpg-w600)

*Avatar*'s effects became the benchmark for the blockbusters that followed. Even now, films still market themselves with “made by *Avatar*'s effects team” or “effects to rival *Avatar*.” Faced with an effects-driven film, audiences will always measure it against *Avatar*; for today's mainstream audience, that comparison has become part of how they pick what to see.

An EntGroup survey found that viewers in first- and second-tier cities and “small-town youth” alike are drawn by visual effects, reviews and genre, and that outer-space science fiction is the genre they like best.

*Avatar* stopped being merely a commercial blockbuster long ago. When the 2015 Beijing International Film Festival screened it again, tickets were as hard to get as for many film classics — in many people's eyes *Avatar* is already a classic of film history. Even on Douban, never kind to commercial films, it holds an 8.6 and ranks 94th on the Douban Top 250.

![A scene from Avatar](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703151739aOZQPi5pkyWmY7Dh.jpg-w600)

Looking back, *Avatar* still falls a little short of the word “masterpiece.” It is a triumph of the American film industry's system, and its great strength is era-defining effects, but the story may be too plain — that, of course, is the argument of the story-first camp. Visually, it really was something new.

One interesting thing: the shock *Avatar* delivered is no different from the moviegoing fever *Star Wars* set off abroad more than thirty years earlier. The crowd *Avatar* drew in China is, at bottom, the same crowd George Lucas drew among young Americans in the 1970s — and that is what set the taste of the whole moviegoing environment.
